leads.name: Speke Hall Yews ("Adam and Eve")
leads.reason: Not researched this pass (over the four-candidate limit set in the brief). Mentioned as 'ancient specimens' by a Liverpool community tree-story project (openeyestories.org.uk). Worth a dedicated look next pass: National Trust property, likely to have its own documentation of these yews' age and history.

leads.name: Sefton Park: no single verifiable specimen found this pass
leads.reason: Searched Wikipedia, Historic England listing (403, blocked), a BSG Ecology restoration survey, Palm House botanical collection page, and three Liverpool naturalist/botanical-society field-trip write-ups. Individual trees mentioned in passing (Atlas Cedar on the lake bank, Caucasian Wingnut near Aigburth Vale/south end of the lake, a 'bong tree' Dawn Redwood, a Weeping Elm near the Fairy Glen, gnarled cherries near the old bandstand) but none with a girth, dated age, or precise location good enough to clear the bar in the time available. Worth a dedicated follow-up pass, ideally starting from a Liverpool Botanical Society Sefton Park field-trip report (their Calderstones report was excellent) or the park's own 150th-anniversary heritage material.

leads.name: Croxteth Hall Walled Garden espaliered fruit trees
leads.reason: The 2-acre Victorian walled garden (built c.1850) holds espaliered pears, apples and peaches against heated flue walls, 'many believed to be at least 100 years old' (Great British Life feature), and is part of the Liverpool Botanical Collection (National Plant Collections). No individual specimen is named with its own age, girth or exact position by any source found. Could work as a compact ensemble entry (one obvious place to stand, the walled garden itself) if a future pass finds a named oldest specimen or a Trust/council source with more detail. The wider deer-park woodland at Croxteth is largely modern Mersey Forest planting (20,000 trees, 2009-2010), not ancient.

leads.name: St James's Cemetery: no single verifiable specimen found this pass
leads.reason: The cemetery itself only dates from 1829 (former stone quarry), so any tree here is under 200 years old. A naturalist group mentions a 'big old Golden Ash' reputed to be in the far south east corner that the group could not actually locate, next to 'an ominous stump', and a mature Tulip Tree also in the south east corner, neither with size or dated-age detail. Not pursued further given the age ceiling and thin sourcing; a council or Friends-of-the-cemetery source might do better.
